headline: Starship's second-stage catch, and the rising price of everything else
paragraphs: SpaceX caught Starship's upper stage with the launch tower's mechanical arms on November 14 (US Central time), which GeekPark describes as the first engineering validation of recovering an orbital-class heavy spacecraft — the first successful second-stage recovery. GeekPark's argument is about cost rather than spectacle: it separates booster return, which begins at roughly 2 km/s and takes 6–7 minutes, from ship re-entry at about 7.8 km/s and roughly 30 minutes, and says full reusability at scale would lower the price of moving mass to and from orbit. That is a claim about a future price, not a published price. China, meanwhile, has laid out its own sequence toward a crewed lunar landing before 2030, with three uncrewed precursor missions first; Wang Xiang, deputy chief designer of the human spaceflight program, presented the plan at a Beijing symposium that opened October 31, and the first, Mengzhou-1, has slipped to early 2027.

The first connecting thread is that the binding constraint in both space and AI is increasingly the cost of moving things — mass to orbit, memory to accelerators, power to data centers. The Financial Times reports buyers of data-center servers being billed up to 45% more than prices agreed months earlier, with memory-heavy CPU nodes doubling or tripling and GPU servers up 20–30%, attributed to the DRAM shortage; one buyer called the gap "disconcerting" and said they absorb it rather than walk away. Amazon reportedly agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for much of Decart, including its optimization software and founding team, a deal Bloomberg reported from one unnamed source and neither company has confirmed; TechCrunch framed it as strengthening the stack behind Amazon's Trainium chips as Amazon prepares to sell that silicon externally. And the New York Times reports, citing unnamed sources, that Elon Musk told SpaceX staff the company is falling behind in AI and that renting data-center capacity to outside customers, including Anthropic, is more lucrative than using it internally — unconfirmed by either company. Penguin Solutions' SC26 demonstration of a photonic memory appliance, adding 576 GB of HBM3E and 16 TB of DDR5 over optical CXL with a 7.2 TB/s bidirectional target, points at the same pressure, but it is a demonstration, not a product shipment.

The second thread is verification. OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra independently produced a Lean proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem that Vals AI, cited by The Decoder, calls the first machine-verifiable proof of the result by any AI; because the needed foundations were absent from Lean's Mathlib, the model devised its own strategy rather than assembling lemmas, and it leads Autoform-Hard with 49 of 56 tasks. The report is secondary and does not describe prompting or review. That matters because a blog post at micjm.com arguing a 17-million-line Lean proof is unusually large set off a Hacker News debate over whether proofs that size can be trusted; commenters warned errors could hide in converted sub-proofs, and a claim the artifact was cut to 13 million lines was not independently verified. METR's updated time-horizon plot sharpens the worry: it reports some capabilities still improving exponentially while models do worse on tasks requiring judgment than on coding, including new open-ended tasks such as designing evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments.

The third thread is that rules are being written by courts, state attorneys general and product settings rather than legislatures. Oregon and Virginia's attorneys general sued several Musk companies, alleging Grok shipped with safeguards too weak to prevent sexualized imagery of real people including children; Wired reported the filings, which have not been tested in court, and the report does not name the defendants or courts. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed on November 22 that companies adopt common development limits using a cross-company metric such as perplexity, disclosing internal figures of about 0.99 for GPT-3.5 and 0.91 for GPT-4, with new cyber and math capabilities appearing below 0.8 — a proposal, not a policy. Walmart's live Agent Gateway, with Meta's Muse as first shopping agent, puts spending limits and purchase approval inside a customer's account, a private substitute for rulemaking. Elsewhere: a Dutch court's interim order stops BYD building or selling the Ti7 in the EU pending trial; the EU Council signals support for voluntary rather than binding corporate EV quotas, per electrive; the Senate passed 62-33 a permitting overhaul letting sponsors of 46 project types sue agencies over bad-faith denials or delays past 60 days; and Rest of World reports IBM ended visa sponsorship for some US employees while offering overseas relocation.

The contradictions are worth holding onto. Zhipu's GLM-5.4 is a 750-billion-parameter model whose 28 twice-computed layers the company says match 2–3 trillion-parameter systems, but the only published benchmark scores come from a 30B test model, and access is gated. Amazon–Decart is a single-source report. Starship's cost case is an argument about what full reusability would do, not a measured price. Watch whether Zhipu releases flagship benchmarks and opens access; whether Amazon confirms Decart and names external Trainium customers; whether the 17-million-line Lean artifact gets an independent audit; how fast Starship flies again; whether Mengzhou-1 holds early 2027; and whether BYD appeals the Dutch order or the EU quotas stay voluntary.
takeaways: The Starship catch is being sold on future launch economics; no price has been published.
AI's near-term bottleneck looks like memory, power and server pricing, not model quality alone.
Machine-checkable proofs are becoming the scoreboard at the same moment their scale makes them hard to check.
